label: Institution
name: Basutoland Congress
summary:
The Basutoland Congress Party (BCP), founded in 1952 by Ntsu Mokhehle in Basutoland (the British protectorate that became Lesotho in 1966), was the principal nationalist movement that led Lesotho's independence campaign and has remained a significant if divided political force in one of the world's most geographically unusual countries — a landlocked kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa.

Basutoland's political status was distinctive in the colonial era: the mountain kingdom (historically the refuge to which Moshoeshoe I rallied the Basotho people from Zulu and Boer pressure in the 1820s-1830s) had avoided direct incorporation into South Africa during the apartheid era — unlike neighboring Bechuanaland (Botswana) and Swaziland, Basutoland maintained British protectorate status partly because its mountain geography made it economically marginal and militarily defensible. This geography gave the BCP's independence campaign particular significance: it was simultaneously obtaining independence and refusing incorporation into apartheid South Africa.

Lesotho's post-independence history has been turbulent: the BCP won the 1965 pre-independence elections but was denied power; subsequent decades saw military coups, electoral fraud, and political instability. Ntsu Mokhehle finally became Prime Minister in 1993 after the BCP won elections; the party later split, with Mokhehle forming the Lesotho Congress for Democracy. Contemporary Lesotho politics features extreme fragmentation among multiple successor parties of the BCP tradition. Lesotho remains the world's only country entirely enclosed within another country at high altitude (it is the only country entirely above 1,000m), a landlocked mountain nation whose political independence from South Africa remains its defining characteristic.
